questions.question: A client has a respiratory rate of 30/min but takes very shallow breaths. Why can PaCO₂ still rise?
choices: Effective alveolar ventilation may be inadequate despite the rapid rate
Every rapid respiratory rate guarantees high tidal volume
Supplemental oxygen automatically removes carbon dioxide
PaCO₂ depends only on hemoglobin concentration
questions.explanation: Alveolar ventilation depends on both rate and the portion of tidal volume reaching gas-exchanging alveoli. Rapid shallow breaths may ventilate mostly dead space and fail to eliminate enough CO₂.

questions.question: Which description best represents a pulmonary shunt?
choices: Blood perfuses alveoli that receive no ventilation
Alveoli are ventilated without any adjacent perfusion
Airflow and perfusion are perfectly matched
Hemoglobin concentration is increased
questions.explanation: In shunt physiology, blood reaches unventilated alveoli or bypasses ventilated alveoli. A large true shunt may respond incompletely to increased inspired oxygen.

questions.question: A pulmonary embolus blocks blood flow to ventilated alveoli. Which mechanism results?
choices: High V/Q and increased alveolar dead space
Low V/Q from excess perfusion
Pure diffusion limitation from fibrosis
Increased oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explanation: The affected alveoli receive ventilation but little or no perfusion, creating high V/Q and wasted ventilation, also called alveolar dead space.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests respiratory muscle fatigue rather than improvement?
choices: A previously distressed client becomes drowsy with slower shallow respirations and less air movement
The client speaks in full sentences with less accessory-muscle use
Breath sounds improve after prescribed bronchodilator therapy
Respiratory rate returns toward baseline while alertness improves
questions.explanation: Falling rate, shallow breathing, reduced air movement, and worsening alertness after sustained distress can signal exhaustion and impending ventilatory failure.

questions.question: Which client requires the most immediate action?
choices: A stable client asking how an incentive spirometer works
A client with a quiet chest, inability to speak, decreasing alertness, and weak respiratory effort
A client with a chronic cough unchanged from baseline
A client awaiting routine pulmonary-function testing
questions.explanation: Minimal air movement, inability to speak, altered alertness, and weak effort indicate critical airflow limitation or respiratory fatigue and require emergency airway and breathing support.

questions.question: Why can a client with severe anemia have tissue hypoxia despite an acceptable PaO₂ and SpO₂?
choices: Total oxygen content is reduced because less hemoglobin is available to carry oxygen
PaO₂ directly measures total hemoglobin concentration
SpO₂ measures cardiac output
Anemia always produces hypercapnia first
questions.explanation: PaO₂ reflects dissolved oxygen pressure and SpO₂ estimates the proportion of hemoglobin saturated. With much less hemoglobin, arterial oxygen content and tissue delivery can still be low.

questions.question: A client receiving supplemental oxygen has an improved SpO₂ but increasing somnolence and shallow respirations. What is the best plan?
choices: Urgently reassess ventilation and prepare for additional airway or ventilatory support
Assume respiratory function is normal because SpO₂ improved
Remove all monitoring
Wait for cyanosis before escalating
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen can improve saturation without correcting hypoventilation. Worsening alertness and shallow breathing require urgent ventilation assessment and escalation.

questions.question: Which action is appropriate when administering oxygen for acute hypoxemia?
choices: Use the ordered delivery system, target the individualized range, and reassess oxygenation, ventilation, and mental status
Withhold oxygen from every client at risk for CO₂ retention
Adjust the device without checking the client or order
Judge response only by the device flow setting
questions.explanation: Indicated oxygen should not be withheld in a hypoxemic emergency. It is titrated to an individualized target with reassessment of the whole respiratory response and possible adverse effects.

questions.question: Which finding best indicates that respiratory support is improving both oxygenation and ventilation?
choices: The client is more alert with less work of breathing and improving oxygen and CO₂ trends
SpO₂ rises while somnolence and PaCO₂ worsen
Respirations become shallower and breath sounds diminish
Blood pressure falls after positive-pressure support
questions.explanation: Improved alertness, reduced effort, and favorable oxygen and carbon-dioxide trends provide converging evidence of benefit. A saturation change alone is incomplete.

questions.question: A client with diffuse inflammatory lung injury has severe hypoxemia, bilateral alveolar opacities, and low lung compliance not fully explained by heart failure. Which mechanism is the priority hypothesis?
choices: ARDS with alveolar–capillary barrier injury and shunt physiology
Isolated increased hemoglobin concentration
Uncomplicated anxiety
Normal age-related change
questions.explanation: ARDS causes inflammatory barrier injury, protein-rich edema, surfactant dysfunction, atelectasis, low compliance, and severe gas-exchange impairment including shunt physiology.
